answer: Yes. The story strikes an appropriate balance between scene and exposition. It unfolds primarily as a vivid, real-time scene—following Clara's immediate actions and sensory experiences as she unlocks the door, walks down the hall, and turns on the kitchen tap—which builds tension and keeps the reader engaged. At the same time, the author seamlessly weaves brief moments of exposition into the descriptions of the setting (mentioning the twenty-year absence, the coffin being carried down the hall, and her mother) to provide necessary background information without slowing the pace or breaking the immersion of the scene.
